question: Will H.R. 33 (United States–Taiwan Expedited Double-Tax Relief Act) be enacted into law before May 1, 2026?
summary: Objections highlight plausible upside from House momentum, a Senate companion, and Treasury-led tax negotiations that could accelerate enactment.
The absence of Senate passage by March 2026 remains the dominant downside risk, keeping the overall probability modest.
Threshold analysis shows enactment by May 1, 2026 is possible but not highly probable, justifying a cautious upward adjustment from the ensemble.

justification.critique_assessment: Objections are valid and reveal a genuine blind spot in the ensemble by signaling momentum and policy framing that could lift odds above the base rate.

forecasts.reference-class: Bipartisan U.S. federal tax-relief legislation involving cross-border taxation with a foreign partner (Taiwan), the enactment of which requires Senate passage and presidential signature.

sources.claim: Forecast on Metaculus assigns a 25% probability that H.R. 33 will be enacted into law before May 1, 2026.
H.R.33 was introduced on January 3, 2025 and, per Congress.gov, received in the Senate and referred to the Committee on Finance (as of January 16, 2025).
Taipei Times reports that the U.S. House passed H.R.33 in January 2025.
Treasury announces that the United States and Taiwan will begin negotiating a comprehensive tax agreement to address double taxation (October 29, 2024).
Senate Foreign Relations and Senate Finance Committees introduced companion U.S.-Taiwan tax legislation, indicating bipartisan momentum.
U.S. Chamber of Commerce expresses strong support for H.R. 33.
H.R.33 was introduced Jan 3, 2025; passed the House Jan 15, 2025; referred to the Senate Finance Committee Jan 16, 2025; no enacted status recorded as of 2026-03.
Text indicates introduction and House action; no indication of enacted status.
Representative McCollum’s statement confirming House passage of H.R.33.
Taipei Times reports House passage of the US-Taiwan Expedited Double-Tax Relief Act by a wide margin (423-1).
Treasury announces start of negotiations on a comprehensive U.S.–Taiwan tax agreement; notes legislative groundwork and implementing steps.
Senate committees introduced companion U.S.–Taiwan tax legislation as a companion to H.R. 33.
All Info shows H.R.33 introduced January 3, 2025, and that the House passed it on January 15, 2025 by a 423-1 vote.
Text indicates the bill was introduced in January 2025 and that the Senate received it on January 16, 2025 (referred to the Senate).
June 4, 2025 press release notes bipartisan Senate action urging consideration of the Taiwan double-tax relief bill.
Taipei Times reports that the US House passed the United States‑Taiwan Expedited Double‑Tax Relief Act with a large bipartisan margin.
All Info page confirms latest action as of January 16, 2025: Senate received and referred to Finance.
ZipDo cites GovTrack data indicating about 12% of bills introduced in the 118th Congress became law within two years.
Brooklyn Law School guide states fewer than 3% of introduced federal bills become law.

causal-factors.name: Senate passage gap (no enacted status in Senate as of 2026-03-01)
causal-factors.rationale: The bill has cleared the House but has not yet gained Senate passage or presidential signature, the main gating step for enactment.

causal-factors.name: House passage and Senate companion momentum
causal-factors.rationale: House approval in January 2025, plus a companion Senate bill introduced soon after, signals bipartisan momentum that could accelerate progress.

causal-factors.name: Treasury-led negotiations on a comprehensive U.S.–Taiwan tax agreement
causal-factors.rationale: Treasury announced the start of negotiations in 2024, framing a path to implementing legislation and a broader tax framework that supports relief efforts.

causal-factors.name: Broad business and bipartisan coalition support
causal-factors.rationale: Strong backing from groups like the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and other bipartisan advocates increases political pressure to move the bill forward.

causal-factors.name: Historical base-rate context for House-passed bills
causal-factors.rationale: Historically, a relatively small share of House-passed bills become law within a two-year window, suggesting caution about near-term enactment.

causal-factors.name: Bipartisan House passage and broad support for H.R.33
causal-factors.rationale: The House passed H.R.33 by a 423-1 vote in January 2025, signaling broad bipartisan support and creating favorable momentum for further action.

causal-factors.name: Senate companion bill and cross-chamber momentum
causal-factors.rationale: Senate committees introduced a companion bill in January 2025, indicating cross-chamber momentum that could translate into Senate action if maintained.

causal-factors.name: Absence of Senate passage by March 1, 2026; Senate inaction risk
causal-factors.rationale: As of 2026-03-01 there is no recorded Senate passage or presidential signature, which historically lowers the odds of enactment for bills that cleared only the House.

causal-factors.name: U.S. Treasury negotiations to address double taxation with Taiwan
causal-factors.rationale: Treasury announced in October 2024 that negotiations would begin on a comprehensive tax agreement, creating a pathway that could support implementation and eventual enactment.

causal-factors.name: Two-stage enactment requirement and Taiwan’s unique status
causal-factors.rationale: H.R.33 envisions an Agreement and accompanying implementing legislation, a process with substantial political and procedural hurdles that could delay or derail enactment.

causal-factors.name: Senate companion introduced (S.199) and cross-chamber momentum
causal-factors.rationale: S.199, a Senate companion to HR33, was introduced on Jan 23, 2025 and referred to the Finance Committee, signaling ongoing bipartisan momentum alongside a House-passed measure. ([congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/199/text?utm_source=openai))

causal-factors.name: House passage of HR33 establishes bipartisan momentum
causal-factors.rationale: The House passed HR33 with wide bipartisan support (423-1) in January 2025, creating a pathway for Senate consideration and signaling strong cross-party backing. ([waysandmeans.house.gov](https://waysandmeans.house.gov/2025/01/16/house-approves-fairer-tax-treatment-for-american-workers-and-manufacturers-strengthening-competitive-edge-against-china/?utm_source=openai))

causal-factors.name: No Senate passage by March 1, 2026 (enactment not yet achieved)
causal-factors.rationale: As of early 2026 there is no enacted HR33/S.199 into law; the Senate companion exists but has not advanced to passage, keeping enactment uncertain within the target window. ([congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/199/all-info?utm_source=openai))

causal-factors.name: Treasury-led move toward a comprehensive US–Taiwan tax agreement
causal-factors.rationale: Treasury announced negotiations toward a broad US–Taiwan tax agreement in Oct 2024, which could create a framework favorable to implementing cross-border tax relief, potentially aiding passage. ([home.treasury.gov](https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/jy2693?utm_source=openai))

causal-factors.name: Bipartisan advocacy and urging Senate action
causal-factors.rationale: Bipartisan letters and statements urging the Senate to take up the bill (e.g., June 2025 letter) underscore ongoing congressional pressure to move toward enactment. ([chu.house.gov](https://chu.house.gov/media-center/press-releases/rep-chu-co-leads-bipartisan-letter-urging-senate-take-taiwan-double-tax?utm_source=openai))

causal-factors.name: Historical baseline: small share of House-passed bills become law
causal-factors.rationale: Historical baselines show a small fraction of House-passed bills ultimately become law, implying downside risk to accelerated enactment despite House support. ([guides.brooklaw.edu](https://guides.brooklaw.edu/federal_legislative_history_research/legislative_process?utm_source=openai))

synthesis: The 9% ensemble understates a measurable upside from cross-chamber momentum and Treasury negotiations, but Senate inaction remains a strong constraint. A modest upward calibration to 13% reflects this balance, with a broad but uncertain window for action by the target date.
